messages:
jess_m: quick question — should new internal control-plane APIs be gRPC+protobuf or stick with JSON/REST for now? thinking about routing policies, quota checks, and console telemetry.

samir: leaning gRPC for perf and streaming (especially for long polling quota updates). fewer bytes, built-in bi-di streams for push.

lee: +1 for binary efficiency but worried about operator UX. our console currently expects JSON logs/events for dashboards. How will we convert telemetry?

noah: we can run a gateway that translates gRPC->JSON for the console. envoy/grpc-gateway are options. tradeoff: extra component to maintain, potential perf penalty at gateway.

jess_m: that's the core of the debate. if we introduce an API gateway, it centralizes auth/rate-limiting too — nice. but adds a single point for diffs in semantics (timeouts, retries).

samir: also generation story: protobufs -> typed clients auto-generated for most languages. That helps platform teams avoid hand-rolling clients. REST + openapi gives similar benefits but tooling is messier across languages.

lee: can we keep a thin REST facade for public endpoints and use gRPC internally between services? That hybrid might give us the best of both worlds.

noah: hybrid is common. caveat: we need clear contracts and versioning strategy. protobuf handles additive changes well, but enums and field renames still bite.

jess_m: what about observability? traces/tags propagate fine over grpc, but our logging/metrics ingestion pipeline expects certain JSON fields. Do we embed structured logs in proto or add a gateway transformer?

samir: prefer embedding structured telemetry in spans (OpenTelemetry) and push OTLP over gRPC. Then the console can read OTLP -> transform into existing dashboard shapes. Avoid stringifying structured logs at service level.

lee: right, but customer-facing audit trails (who changed routing policies) should still be readable JSON in the DB. So we should serialize those events as JSON blobs at the write edge.

jess_m: rollout concerns: switching wire format is risky. proposal: start with a new service (quota-service v2) implemented gRPC internally, keep current REST endpoints for consumers for 6 months, then deprecate. Canary via Redwood Console rollout UI.

noah: agree. also add a compatibility layer in the gateway that can respond to both proto and json requests during canary. simple content-negotiation header.

samir: question: do we use streaming for quota updates or just server-sent events? gRPC streaming is nice but existing JS frontend support is awkward (websockets needed).

lee: frontend can subscribe via the gateway over SSE/WS. backend-to-backend can use gRPC streaming. So split concerns: use gRPC streaming for internal fanout, translate to SSE for browser.

jess_m: TL;DR draft plan: 1) adopt protobufs+gRPC for new internal service-to-service APIs, 2) implement gateway (envoy + grpc-gateway) to expose JSON REST/SSE for clients and console, 3) use OTLP over gRPC for telemetry, 4) generation + linters for backward-compatible proto changes, 5) staged rollout with gateway compatibility + canary.

samir: I like it. can we add a checklist for infra: HTTP/2 readiness on our LB, per-route timeouts in envoy, quota plugin placement (gateway vs service)?

noah: added: health-check semantics for streaming, circuit-breakers, and retries policy docs. I can sketch a PR for the repo.

lee: small UX ask: console should show "protocol" column in service registry so SRE knows which services speak gRPC vs REST. Also expose per-endpoint request/response sizes in dashboard.

jess_m: good point. I'll create an RFC and include perf numbers expected from a small prototype. if you want to prototype, try a simple quota-service gRPC + envoy gateway and measure p95 and tokens/sec.

infra-bot: deploy requested: canary/quota-service-v2 scheduled for 1779991288 by noah — status: pending.

noah: thanks — will push a minimal proto and envoy config this afternoon. will tag you in the RFC once ready.

samir: :thumbsup:

lee: :eyes:

jess_m: thanks all — keeping this thread as the discussion record.
